text: Take on Irreplaceable You (2018 movie). So, on a random Sunday, I came across this movie, and my decision to watch it was largely based on its poster. There was a cute girl sitting on the shoulders of a cute, clean-shaven guy with a very prominent dimple. What can I say? The poster did its job. Going into the movie, I was expecting a deep, moving love story. Sam and Abbie had the history to make it one: childhood sweethearts who had been together for nearly two decades. But somehow, that love never quite translated onto the screen. Or maybe I just didn't get it. Abbie seemed determined to stay in control of Sam's life, deciding who he should date, when he should move on, and even who would take care of him. Sam, on the other hand, seemed rather lost when it came to Abbie. He didn't quite know how to support her or navigate what was happening between them. And then there was Dominic, the nurse, who somehow seemed more emotionally invested in Abbie than Sam did. By the end, Sam's marriage proposal felt less like a declaration of love and more like an act of pity. Perhaps that wasn't the intention, but that's how it came across to me. For a couple who had spent almost their entire lives together, I expected to feel their love. Unfortunately, I was left wondering whether I had missed something or whether the movie had. Let me know what you think of it.

text: After waiting a year for HOPE to come out, I finally saw it last night and loved it, then did my usual thing of checking out what other people are saying on Reddit and the like—and I am a bit appalled. This, as they say, is why we can't have nice things. People keep making ridiculous suggestions that the film is a parody of the action genre (it's not, though it is a subversion of it), or that the story is "all over the place" (pfft), etc. Nonsense. This is not one of those dumb action films somebody started without a script because such-and-such was only available through May. It's a smart movie, made by someone with a track record of making smart movies, and worth engaging with. So let's do a breakdown of what this film's about and some of the elements I enjoyed about it. As a note, I'm not Korean, but I spent a couple years in Korea, so I probably got more out of it than a lot of international viewers and a lot less than native ones. It is of course possible that I have misinterpreted some of its points. That said, I am a professionally published writer myself, albeit nobody important, meaning I at least know what themes and motifs are and I don't misuse the term "plot hole." I've also watched all of Na's stuff and a fair number of other Korean movies, so I recognize some Korean cinema tropes. THE STORY: INFILTRATION: When the movie opens, we find ourselves to be in a village close to the North Korean border. Signs everywhere warn residents to watch for infiltrators from the North and report anyone suspicious. If such signs were shown just once we might brush them aside as scene-setting, but they pop up multiple times, so we know they matter. This is a movie about our fear of others. THE HUNTERS: But who are the others? North Korean spies are the first others that get mentioned, but the first ones that we actually see are the hunters. One of the hunters mentions that it doesn't matter if the chief of police gets mad at him because he's getting "back on the boat" soon, which probably means he's one of the ethnic Koreans from Northeast China. Na Hong-Jin has made a movie about the plight of some of these people (THE YELLOW SEA, 2010); they come to South Korea by boat to work illegally. THE ALIENS: Of course, the star infiltrators of the movie are the aliens. The first alien is depicted as a vicious monster rampaging through town before we find out that it was just looking for its child and was murdered for its trouble. THE CONFLICT: The humanization of the aliens in this movie results in an unusual emotional conflict during the movie's action sequences. "HOPE": At the movie's end, we start getting translations of the aliens' dialogue, and a new plot seems to come out of nowhere regarding the death of the aliens' emperor and the need to find their prince. CONCLUSION: What we have here is a film about our fear of the other, particularly immigrants, and the awful things we do to them rather than understand them or reach out a helping hand. OK, that's the meaning I got. THE UNKILLABLE MAN: The hunter Ko Sung-ki appears to be immortal; every time he receives a blow that is likely to kill him, he gets up again. THE UNEXPECTED BAD-ASS: Officer Yim arrives on the scene in action-movie bad-ass mode, striking the first serious blow against an alien after it's devastated the town. THE SHERIFF: Hwang Jung-min plays Ko as a police chief who likes to throw his weight around a bit. At the end of the movie he says he "feels weird" (in the English subtitles). We should, too.
label: analysis

text: My theory that the dog "Precious" in Silence of the Lambs is a subtle Hobbit/Lord of the Rings reference. I had some interesting observations last night when I was watching Silence of the Lambs. Firstly, in the final climatic scene of film, we see Agent Starling enter the basement level of the house of Buffalo Bill. As she descends into the basement after Bill, she discovers his hostage Catherine Martin at the bottom of the well. As she peers down into the well, she see a scared and dirty Catherine clutching tightly Bill's white Bichon Frise dog "Precious". Starling immediately lets out a gasp of 'Oh God' when she sees this. Precious is barking and barking, and Starling even goes as far to yell at Catherine saying "Now shut that dog up" and tells the girl to shut up too. What we can draw from this is that, symbolically, Precious is the lamb and Catherine is a young version of Starling. Precious even looks like a little white lamb, all puffy and white. As such, Precious's barking becomes the 'screaming of the lambs'. Just as Hannibal said to Starling, "You still wake up sometimes, don't you, you wake up in the dark hearing the screaming of the lambs". And just like in her dream, Bill cuts the lights, leaving her in the dark, scared and cold. Furthermore, another aspect of 'Precious' the dog I have never seen mentioned is the dog as a symbol for 'Precious', the ring from Hobbit/Lord of the Rings, which would cast Buffalo Bill as a 'Gollum' like character. Bill even talks to the dog in a similar way that Gollum talks to the ring, calling it "My Precious" over and over. Meanwhile, this would cast Catherine as a sort of Bilbo reference, where she uses trickery to steal Precious away from Bill, which sets him into an insane murderous rage. I am interested to hear what people think.
label: analysis

text: By absurdism, I am referring to Camus' philosophy, summarized from Wikipedia here- "Absurdism is the philosophical theory that the universe is irrational and meaningless. It states that trying to find meaning leads people into conflict with a seemingly meaningless world." Relevant quote from Camus' The Stranger about the dark wind rising from the future. Mike originally tries to create meaning by seeking ego-driven pursuits. But finding them unsatisfying, he is constantly searching for more meaning. When he first encounters Joan's tribe, he is mesmerized by their conviction and values. However when he meets Joan's father, he is once again confronted with the uncomfortable dialectic of mankinds desperate search for meaning and objectivity which will never be found. Joan makes a salient point to him that everything in his life is fake, and death is the only thing that will have real stakes and meaning in his existence. By the end of the movie, when Mike's ego-driven actions have paid off and he is at his most popular, he decides it doesn't matter anymore. Life is absurd. So he thrusts himself into the volcano. Not saying this was a brilliant movie or anything like that. But if there is a deeper philosophy to it I think absurdism fits pretty well. To me, a lot of the humor came from the protagonist being such a naive idiot on the path to arriving at an absurdist philosophy on life.
label: analysis

text: TL;DR: If the themes, energy, and stylistic flourishes of 28 Years Later clicked with you, T2 Trainspotting is worth revisiting. The creative DNA between them is stronger than I expected. Back in 2017 though, T2 Trainspotting didn't hit the same way. I was not a huge fan of the original Trainspotting. When they try to break the glass.... water fills the holes up and acts like a barrier. The performances by these two should win them awards and I think these two performances will absolutely be overlooked when it comes to award season simply due to their streaming-exclusivity. The climax of this movie is this family of 4 fighting this giant octo-alien to the death like some homemade Call of Duty game. It's original, it's entertaining, there are great performances by all actors involved, it tugs at your heartstrings while also freaking you the fuck out. text: My first exposure to Taylor Sheridan was 2015's Sicario. Directed by Denis Villeneuve, Sicario is a bleak story about the ultimate collapse of jurisdiction, legality, and morality around the War on Drugs. It has been called the Apocalypse Now of the War on Drugs. The year after, 2016, saw the release of Hell or High Water, directed by David Mackenzie. Hell or High Water is a great film, as all of the performances, settings, and dialogue create a sincere and disturbing look at rural poverty in America. The climactic refrain of the film is poignant, "I've been poor my whole life, like a disease passing from generation to generation. But not my boys, not anymore." And the year after that we have 2017's Wind River, directed by Sheridan himself. It tackles the murder of Indigenous women on western reservations with appropriate weight and despair. The climactic standoff absolutely deserves its place in film history, and it features an incredible performance by Gil Birmingham. By 2018 Sheridan had three critically acclaimed films under his belt. Then he writes the superfluous sequel to Sicario titled Sicario: Day of the Soldado, which failed to make any real impact at all. And then Yellowstone happens, which launches Sheridan into the stratosphere in terms of fame and income. I hate Yellowstone. I hate how its understanding of the west is seemingly entirely based in the Texan hatred of public land and land conservation. In Wind River oil rig workers were the racist, murdering, rapists, in Landman they're heroes holding up the American way of life. But I know the answer already. It's money. Soap Operas aimed at suburban conservatives sell very well, and Yellowstone is the apotheosis of that genre.
label: analysis

text: Question, Which film is better, Fail Safe or Dr. Strangelove? I re-watched Dr. Strangelove recently, and I have re-watched this film so many times. It truly is a great film, in large part because of the performances. Peter Sellers gives a master performance, George C. Scott gives a legendary performance, Slim Pickens, Sterling Hayden all great. What also made the film great is just how absurd the whole film is, and how Kubrick realized just how absurd the whole Nuclear Conflict is. Dr. Strangelove, to me, is a perfect, and probably one of Kubrick's Best. On Fail Safe, I must admit, I only heard of this film because of Dr. Strangelove and how Kubrick & Peter George sued the production because they felt it infringed on Red Alert, the source material. I heard people talk positively over the film, and I gotta say, It's a great film. While Dr. Strangelove is absurd, Fail Safe takes the whole premise seriously. Sidney Lumet masterfully directs the film, the performances are top notch, and I think the best performance was Henry Fonda. You can tell the film was shot very cheaply, and that Lumet had to shoot in own backyard, but I think it adds to the grittiness of the film. I'll give the edge to Dr. Strangelove. The Performances in Dr. Strangelove are just very memorable but I will admit, I was surprised with Fail Safe. What do you think, Which film is better, Fail Safe or Dr. Strangelove?

text: Hi everyone! I'm working on a research project for my masters about the relationship between reading a book and watching its film adaptation, specifically focusing on how people imagine fictional spaces while reading and how those mental images compare with the spaces presented on screen. When a film adaptation comes along, it presents us with a concrete visual interpretation of those spaces. Sometimes the locations look almost exactly as we imagined them; other times, they look completely different. Does seeing a film's version of a place change how we remember or imagine it? Do we feel disappointed when a location doesn't match our mental image, or can the filmmaker's interpretation become even more convincing than our own? For this project, I'm particularly interested in The Lord of the Rings, since Tolkien's descriptions of Middle-earth have inspired readers to imagine its landscapes in their own ways, while Peter Jackson's film trilogy offers a highly recognizable visual interpretation of that world. I'm hoping to find at least 50 people who have both read The Lord of the Rings and watched its film adaptations and would be willing to participate in a short survey. If you've both read the books and watched the films please let me know in the comments! If you have any thoughts on this topic, I'd also love to hear them.

text: My Deep Analysis of The Neon Demon, Entirely Subjective. Heard this movie was both booed and applauded at Cannes. Watching it for the first time, I booed it myself, but on multiple viewings I can say I'll be the one clapping for its craft now. Refn's sheer craft really elevates this film. In most scenes where Jesse exists alongside other cast members, a clear visual line separates her from them, showing her alienation and outsider status. In the party scene, a pillar divides her from Sarah and Gigi. In the bathroom scene following it, another pillar does it. In the tryout scene, the window creates a clear division between Jesse and Sarah. The animal symbolism also goes deeper than I first noticed. Jesse's room is obliterated by a cougar, and Ruby's house has a cheetah replica, shown behind her own reflection in the mirror. After Ruby, Gigi, and Sarah "consume" Jesse, a wolf replica appears behind Ruby. Jesse is the lamb, and Ruby, Gigi, and Sarah are the wolves, beautiful women who devour other beauties to sustain their own. The morning after is shot with a strikingly calm, cool tone, pale blues, quiet sunlight, where every other morning scene in the film up to that point is warm and golden. The triangle's color shifts from blue to red, marking the exact point she matures into something harder, more narcissistic. My real critique of this movie is that it leans on some scenes and sequences that don't fully explain themselves, and the character development stalls at points.
label: analysis

text: UNDERTONE - Review: A Decent Sonic Trip, But All Sound and No Substance. Undertone hits exactly where it promises to-your eardrums-but unfortunately, it doesn't leave much of an impression anywhere else. As an auditory horror experience, it's a perfectly decent ride, but it ultimately collapses under the weight of its own hype, leaving behind a trail of convoluted plotlines and frustratingly lazy ambiguity. The movie's sound design is its biggest selling point, making a good pair of headphones an absolute requirement. The slow, sweeping camera pans are genuinely anxiety-inducing at first. However, the film quickly falls into the trap of overusing its best asset. If you've been thoroughly "ruined" by modern horror masterpieces like The Haunting of Hill House or Hereditary, Undertone is going to test your patience. Those projects trained us to constantly scan every single inch of the frame, hunting for hidden ghosts during a slow pan. Undertone mimics that exact visual tension but completely forgets the payoff. Between a highly derivative story, middle-of-the-road acting, and horror elements that feel forced around an audio gimmick, Undertone just doesn't have any replay value.
label: analysis

text: David Lynchs Lost Highway. Gripping, heavy, overwhelming. Lynch and Gifford formed a wonderful artistic partnership, one that resulted in a cohesive and coherent screenplay for Lost Highway. A two-part film, part horror, part noir, with a massive shift at its midpoint. The opening time-lapse sequence on the highway immediately had me completely captivated with its hypnotic quality. Especially in this first part of the film, I felt countless echoes of Eraserhead. The Mystery Man appears as an otherworldly entity, similar to the Lady in the Radiator from Eraserhead or the Man from Another Place from Twin Peaks. To me, he is definitely a part of Fred's subconscious. The film's circular logic and its ending ultimately reveal: such an obsession condemns us to repeat all of our mistakes over and over again. A few words about the soundtrack: Angelo Badalamenti's score, David Bowie's "I'm Deranged," Lou Reed's "This Magic Moment," Marilyn Manson's "Apple of Sodom," Rammstein's "Rammstein" - these songs become one with the sound design. A masterpiece.

text: Racist protagonists and trauma-dumping! I've noticed a highly specific narrative device in three films where the racist protagonist is humanized and granted victimhood by a backstory where he was traumatized or suffered a loss due to violent colored people. WHO FRAMED ROGER RABBIT (1987) lets the hardboiled detective have had his brother murdered by a cartoon character as an explanation for his racism against cartoon characters, while the source novel's racial segregation metaphor is removed. AMERICAN HISTORY X (1998) builds its entire plot around a flashback dinner table monologue by the father about affirmative action, before the father is shot dead by a black drug dealer. Using a tragic backstory to grant empathy for an amoral character is a narrative device, and a blunt one at that. Personally I think it is okay to dismiss the person. Racism represents an actual threat to other people.

text: Buddy (2026): Not the best horror of the year, but a solid showing. What I liked most about Buddy was that I was pleasantly surprised by the worldbuilding involved. Instead of a murderer-in-a-mascot-costume kind of thing, what we got was an eldritch-horror-in-a-mascot-costume. Many people read Buddy as a metaphor for abuse and the way abusers control their environment and the people around them. The scene where Buddy gropes Nurse Grace is emblematic of this: he is more interested in power and control than anything else. But there's also a compelling case to be made that Buddy is about the way we treat and view children, and the lessons imparted on them by media and society. Buddy takes care to highlight the sing-alongs about doing chores, about staying in line. The one piece of criticism I agree with is that child deaths occur in this movie, and they always feel a little cheap. All in all, I found this a fairly strong movie if not a perfect one. I give it a solid 8.5/10.

text: Is it a moral failure if a filmmaker tries to communicate a cultural idea without fully fleshing out the characters that represent that culture? I see a fair amount of outrage towards films that try to communicate certain ideas about race, gender, sexual orientation, class, etc, when the characters that embody those demographics are more of an idea than a fully fleshed out character. I'm finding myself a bit torn, because on one hand it is always better to have well realized representations of all types of people. On the other hand, if the idea is still effectively communicated, I consider it a net positive. I'm thinking of this with James Gray's Armageddon Time in mind. I felt very deeply for the character of Johnny, a black boy that the Jewish protagonist (Paul) befriends. The film may not fully explore the inner world of Johnny, and instead focuses on his position in Paul's world and the aggressions Paul witnesses him face. text: Review: Big Deal on Madonna Street [1958]. There's something so quaintly beautiful about a simple, human-level comedy that relies on well-timed delivery over goofy spectacle. Big Deal on Madonna Street has a certain antique charm, combining the bumbling wholesomeness of The Three Stooges with the grittiness of Neorealism. It starts with a failed car theft, where Cosimo is arrested by police. While incarcerated, he overhears a crooked bricklayer's plan to rob a safe. Cosimo arranges for Peppe to falsely confess and serve his time for him, only for both men to be thrown in jail instead. They're a ragtag group of wannabe gangsters who are constantly at each other's throats, never menacingly. Their plan and execution consists of a series of gags, hijinks, snappy one-liners, and dry banter. Piero Umiliani's jazzy score apparently set the stage for the quintessential sounds of European cinema through the sixties and seventies. Its characters are flawed yet real, its themes are timeless and universal.

Haruka loses basically everything: her family, her sense of safety, her future. The revenge isn't presented as some satisfying "getting even" fantasy either. It feels more like watching someone who has lost everything trying to find a reason to keep going. And the ending was fantastic, I genuinely didn't see it going in that direction. text: Bring Her Back Isn't About Love. It's About Something Much Worse: Grief and Finality. Laura has won. Piper is underwater. The ritual is almost complete. And suddenly, at the exact moment of manifestation, Laura stops. Discourse surrounding the film favors a specific interpretation: that Bring Her Back explores the lengths we're willing to go to hold onto love. However, Cathy's death never prevented Laura from loving her. What explains Laura's behavior is something far more savage than "love gone too far." Grief persists. It's non-linear in its approach. The resurrection ritual can be understood as Laura's grief, converted into instrumental behavior. The impossible imperative of bereavement becomes a horrifyingly feasible project. Then Piper calls Laura "Mum." And Laura stops. At precisely the moment the resurrection becomes attainable, Laura receives what she believed only the resurrection could provide. Rather than complete the resurrection, Laura releases Piper and allows her to escape. After releasing Piper, Laura carries Cathy into the pool and dies alongside her. Grief for the bereaved requires irreversibility because adaptation requires some relatively fixed fact around which the organism can reorganize itself. Bring Her Back is about what happens when grief is given agency against the very fact that ordinarily allows it to integrate into our lives.
label: analysis

text: How do you portray Black resistance without turning history into revenge fantasy? I've been thinking about why the Montgomery Riverfront Brawl footage stuck with so many people. It puts a Black FBI agent at the center of a Civil Rights-era story in Mississippi and pairs him with a Mafia informant when the usual legal process isn't getting results. text: The Remains of the Day is one of the greatest adaptations ever. The Remains of the Day is an excellent adaptation in every respect, that uses the language of cinema to convey the ideas, themes, and motifs of its source material without feeling encumbered by it. Kazuo Ishiguro's original novel is particularly difficult to adapt because so much of the book centres around Stevens' reflections presented using his inner voice. The film overcomes these challenges and succeeds for two primary reasons. The first is Anthony Hopkins' performance as Stevens, who makes non-expression expressive through pauses, posture, and microscopic changes in facial expression. The second is subtle choices by which Stevens' inner thoughts from the book are conveyed through dialogue or interactions with other characters, such as the story about the butler who shot a tiger beneath his master's dining table. The film has Stevens' father recount it to the rest of the staff in Stevens' presence while making clear that Stevens has heard it before and nods along approvingly, establishing that the story is already part of Stevens' understanding of himself.

text: Se7en, Cure, Angel Heart & True Detective belong to a genre that doesn't really have a name. text: My Problem with Nolan, The Odyssey and Why Dark Knight was the WORST Thing to Happen to Him. Nolan's strength is plot, and having story-driven movies that are more self contained. So now we have The Dark Knight, where despite how it helped to elevate the Superhero movie and gave us one of the great characters in Joker, the main character was weak and not well written, the fight choreography was incredibly weak and the exposition led to a very derivative story that TOLD more than it SHOWED. The immense success of that film made Nolan think he should be making big event, blockbuster films that rely on dynamic visuals and more elaborate action scenes - two aspects that Nolan is not strong at. So when we come to the Odyssey, you see how the visuals are drab, the action scenes are lacking and you don't really connect with Odysseus in the way David Lean made us go on a journey with Lawrence or Maximus in Gladiator.

text: This is what cinema is. [The Shawshank Redemption] I had been putting off watching The Shawshank Redemption for quite some time, and finally I watched it. The movie raised this question for me: how we have grown accustomed to think that intelligence is flashy, real power is loud and charismatic, but Andy shows us the other way around. How hope of seeing a friend and shaking his hand, how hope of seeing the hotel your friend said he would build, how those promises keep us moving in life, how that very promise kept Red moving forward and how he didn't end up like Brooks, the movie lets us feel that hope.

text: Rewatched 'Under the Skin' and legitimately think it might be my current favorite film. After rewatching it just a few days ago, I honestly think it's one of the most raw, primal examples of what the entire medium of film is capable of. The backgrounds of the aliens environments are literally depicted as being completely black and completely white. The aliens exist in a world of hyper, stark objectivity, where there is no sense of value to life, just the consumption of it. I noticed another interesting theme, which is the way that all four elements play a very distinct role in the aliens experience: Earth - the first moment where the alien is taken out of its sense of control is when it trips and falls on the ground. Water - the surfer and the family on the beach being swept away serving as the ultimate proof that it is not human. Air - the wall of mist representing the alien's ultimate seduction into trying to be human. Fire - the attacker in the woods, finding out the truth and seeing the alien's true form, chooses to set it alight, the 'baptism/cleansing by flame' serving as the punishment for the sin of pretending to be human.
label: analysis

text: "The Odyssey" is far from the visual treat I was expecting. While I was watching it, all I could think of was this did not look like the work of a confident director, but of someone that's (way too) confident in his 'directorial brand'. The shots at sea, for instance, are screaming for the audience to be in awe of the technical difficulties. But other than a couple of standout sequences, namely the superbly staged act featuring Samantha Morton as Circe, the movie itself is visually unremarkable and below Nolan's standards. The visual symmetry of "Dunkirk" is gone. The battle scenes are generically choreographed, and the mise en scène was lacking even in crucial interior shots, including the climax. I'll mention one element of the picture that clearly stands out: the elegance and precision of Ludwig Göransson's score, which Nolan's directorial achievement never quite matches.

text: A coyote moves through the streets in Collateral. He kills whoever he pleases, based on a calculation of what benefits him. Vincent: "Now we gotta make the best of it, improvise, adapt to the environment, Darwin, shit happens, I ching, whatever man, we gotta roll with it." The director has stated that his intention with the film is to awaken some of the wildness lurking beneath the polished, neon-lit surface. Whereas the coyote of North American mythology represents the power capable of dismantling the persona-mask that our present society guards so zealously, the wolf in the Norse mythology represents the power needed to face what this dismantling reveals.

text: Snowpiercer (2013) is not trying to depict a 1-to-1 allegory for our society, which is what makes it interesting. Wilford shaped his train society to be the way it is because he does not know how to lead, govern, or do much else besides hide behind massive wealth. He created a 'capitalist hell' because he was too lazy to figure out how to actually lead a nation and he knew the only true threat posed to him was overpopulation. People have criticized the movie for falling apart logically when you actually think about people working and living on a train, but the train completely failed as a society because it blew up before it was old enough to vote.

text: Why would Nikki be in trouble at the end of Obsession? SPOILERS. I have only heard takes pitying Nikki's plight at the end of Obsession. Even the director has said in interviews she's "going to jail" because all the evidence suggests Nikki murdered three people. I would contend that this isn't necessarily true, as an alternative narrative could be spun wherein it was Bear who murdered Sarah and Ian, and then killed himself with the pills, leaving Nikki alive. Why wouldn't Nikki just explain that Bear used the One Wish Willow on her? It's plainly a known thing in-universe. The used willow and its box is literally in the room at the end, the number on the back works, the store employees can attest that it works. The film wants to have its cake and eat it too: the One Wish Willow is simultaneously taken for granted as being real by the store employees, to the point they're bored by it, and as something no one believes can possibly work.
label: analysis

text: Thoughts on The End of Oak Street (& The Shining). I believe there are some notable parallels between Kubrick and David Robert Mitchell in that each film of theirs is a wholly unique genre. I sensed that Greg's (Ewan McGregor) alcoholism was thematically similar to Jack Torrance's alcoholism in The Shining, in that it was this hidden mechanic that predated the film's timeline but reappeared in the middle of it. I also clocked that the sledge hammer looked and functioned like the axe Jack wields in The Shining. While Jack uses his against his family, Greg uses his weapon to defend his family. In my read, the dinosaurs & prehistoric land represent the same externalized supernatural element that the ghosts & Overlook Hotel did in The Shining. Both the Overlook and Oak Street serve as physical containers for these ephemeral internal fears that center on our shared ancient, violent, uncontrollable animalistic urge.

text: Blue Velvet (1986): Worth Watching, But I Don't Get the Hype. I recently watched both Blue Velvet and Mulholland Drive for the first time. My biggest issue was with Frank Booth. I know he's widely regarded as one of cinema's greatest villains, but I simply couldn't take him seriously. His dialogue and erratic behavior struck me as so exaggerated that they often crossed the line from unsettling into unintentionally comical. Unlike many of Lynch's later works, Blue Velvet also felt surprisingly conventional - essentially a fairly straightforward crime thriller with a heavy dose of bizarre sexual content. The film places so little emotional emphasis on Dorothy's family that, by the time the climax arrives, it's difficult to feel invested in their fate. That said, Angelo Badalamenti's score is fantastic, and I also found Kyle MacLachlan's performance as Jeffrey to be rather subdued, which came across as somewhat bland compared to the larger-than-life personalities surrounding him.

text: Did Auggie mistake keeping her hands clean for doing the right thing? This is my main point of disagreement with The 3 Body Problem. What concerns me is Auggie's response after the Panama operation. When Auggie walks away, I don't see it as taking the moral high ground; it feels like she is giving up her influence over future difficult decisions. Imagine a train heading toward eight billion people. The first measure to slow it down costs 1,000 lives, horrific, yet necessary. One engineer witnesses the sacrifice and walks away, but another stays, knowing that leaving means losing the chance to influence what happens next. My criticism is not that she should have been more ruthless, but that she confuses keeping her conscience clean with fulfilling her responsibility. In contrast, I found Jin's arc more compelling. Did anyone else interpret Auggie this way, or do you believe walking away was the genuinely more ethical choice?

text: A more disturbing version of Obsession? What if Bear got his real wish? I think the general consensus is that this is a film about violation of consent which showcases Bear's actions as morally wrong. But one thing that stood out to me was that the willow failed to deliver Bear's actual wish. Bear wished for Nikki to love him, but in fact she never did. I would like to propose a retelling where instead of subjugating her conscious mind, the willow wish instead rewires Nikki's brain and causes her to truly love Bear, through and through. In this version, Bear still commits the evil act of using magic power to force a woman's consent, but there is no bizarre behavior nor overt horror that follows, and no negative consequences for Bear. This version would be difficult to market as a horror film, and yet this story is perhaps more sinister and deeply disturbing than the original. The villain wins and his victim is happy that he did.

text: The way in which audiences view film adaptations is fundamentally broken. When it comes to criticising adaptations of IP and literature, there is an expectation for the film to function as the definitive interpretation and version of the original work. To illustrate, I'm going to use a movie I consider bad: Man of Steel. If I were to explain why I hate this movie, I would talk about its terrible misuse of non-linear storytelling. Yet I've never had an issue with the aspect most criticised: that Jonathan Kent tells him that perhaps he should've let those kids die. I see this same line of thinking when it comes to Tom Holland's Spider-Man: Homecoming trilogy. There is plenty to criticise - the flat cinematography, the indistinct directing. But I don't understand the criticisms that 'Spider-Man's villains should not be connected to Tony Stark' or that 'Spider-Man shouldn't be using technology.' Each adaptation should be treated like a distinct vision of an artist.
label: analysis

text: The Odyssey, Emily Wilson, and the difference between Review and Critique. What we are all witnessing is more-or-less the narcissism of small differences being played out between two highly competent researchers at different ends of their field. Nolan is engaging with philology through adaptation and that's the exact angle from which Wilson has chosen to attack. The problem then becomes that the blockbuster viewing population doesn't have the context to unpack a conversation like this with the depth that it requires. The former [a review] is entirely about opining in such a way that tells you whether or not you should see a film - the latter [a critique] is about understanding its mechanisms. Wilson is critiquing, but most are engaging with it as strictly a review. This disjunction is where I feel most are getting stuck: why would she say that there are aspects of The Odyssey which are racist or sexist, yet still recommend its viewing at the end?
label: analysis

text: What happens when a documentary is completed nearly fifty years after it was filmed? NOVA '78 is a documentary constructed from footage shot by Howard Brookner during the 1978 Nova Convention in New York, bringing together William S. Burroughs, Patti Smith, Laurie Anderson, Allen Ginsberg and others. The documentary he might have made was never completed, and much of the footage remained unseen for decades. At what point does an archival documentary stop being the work of the original filmmaker and become the work of those who rediscover, edit and complete it? Is this an act of preservation, interpretation, authorship, or some combination of all three? I'm one of the producers on the film, so I'm obviously not a neutral observer, but I'm genuinely interested in how people here think about this. text: 30 for 30. My breakdown of the best 30 Japanese movies of the last 30 years, with reviews for each. I've spent the last 18 months deep diving into modern Japanese cinema. When you deep dive like this, you start to notice patterns between films - alienation, societal norms, unanswered family tensions, school pains, dissatisfied wives. Love Exposure (2008) Sion Sono - simply put, is the War & Peace of extreme cinema. Eureka (2000) Shinji Aoyama - a sepia-toned character study about the lasting effects of a violent rampage on its only survivors. Cure (1997) Kiyoshi Kurosawa - one of the creepiest films ever put to celluloid. Spirited Away (2001) Hayao Miyazaki - this movie is all journey, all experience, and all image. Battle Royale (2000) Kinji Fukusaku - the director said he was inspired to adapt the novel because he remembered working in a munitions factory during world war two. Drive My Car (2021) Ryusuke Hamaguchi - an epic meditation on grief. Audition (1999) Takashi Miike - positions itself at first as an offbeat romantic comedy, and then very much as an excruciating horror show. Shoplifters (2018) Hirokazu Koreeda - what is more important, blood relations or genuine care and compassion? Let me know what you've seen, what you agree with, and what you don't.

text: I watched Juno again at 33, and I have a fresh take. Juno doesn't know who she is. She finds the beginning of an answer in Mark - a man in his 30s who is a model of adulthood. Vanessa, for the entirety of the film, has this anxiety about her, all related to her desire to become a mother in spite of her infertility. We see her control their anniversary photos on the wall, she controls how much space within the house Mark's life is allowed to occupy. This shows that Mark is actually a feature of the house, rather than a partner in his own right. When Juno meets Mark, she sees in him a model of healthy adulthood, and when Mark meets Juno, he gets reminded of what it feels like to have someone truly take an interest in your world. Juno's parents, Mac and Bren, understand through hard-won experience that messy relationships happen, outside of anyone's control.

The locations take you from mountains, to beaches, to the city, to interiors of old houses, to jungles. text: My thoughts on The Odyssey. I don't like Nolan's films, so I wasn't expecting much, and in any case, I didn't like it. text: Nolan's Last Four Films Are A Tetralogy About Human Warfare. 1 The Opening: Odyssey (Classical Warfare) 2 The Companion: Dunkirk (Modern Warfare) 3 The Penultimate: Oppenheimer (Pre-Nuclear) 4 The Final: Tenet (Post-Nuclear). It begins with the regional, mythological conflict depicted in The Odyssey, where warfare is fought with classical cold weapons. It then develops into the large-scale modern warfare of the First World War, as portrayed in Dunkirk. Oppenheimer marks the escalation of advanced nuclear research, while planting the seeds of humanity's potential apocalyptic fate. Finally, it ends in Tenet, where humanity attempts to save itself from thermodynamic annihilation. I also noticed that the opening and final parts of this tetralogy are fictional, while the two middle parts are based on historical events.
label: analysis

text: Would Titanic still resonate with people if released today? Upon a recent rewatch I noticed that this iconic love story of cinema lasts only for a period of about 4 days, from the time Jack meets Rose till the sinking. In 4 days Jack and Rose meet and form such a deep connection where Jack is ready to give up his life for Rose, and similarly Rose is ready to leave everything in her life behind for Jack. My question is would such a love story still be bought by audiences in 2026? I think one of the counters is that both are teenagers (Jack is 19 and Rose is 17) and teenage love can be like that. Silly and intense. I was slightly amused that the story of Jack and Rose is considered so popular and iconic but it only was an affair that lasted 4 days, and a few meetings.
label: analysis

text: Is there a recurring theme of violence against women in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey? Throughout the movie, it felt like women were constantly suffering because of the actions of men. Agamemnon's daughter is sacrificed to further the goals of Agamemnon. Penelope is essentially held hostage by men who want to use her to gain power, and she even has a speech about how people don't take her seriously as a leader despite ruling on her own for 20 years. Circe is heavily implied to be a victim of violence at the hands of men, soldiers who fought in the Trojan War. Calypso dedicates seven years of her life to caring for what is basically a stranger, only to be abandoned. Helen is left mutilated and treated like a trophy, degraded by her own husband Menelaus for her facial scars. Did anyone else pick up on this, or am I just seeing patterns that aren't really there?
label: analysis

text: Black Swan and the voyeuristic gaze: does Nina become dissociated from her own body because she has learned to constantly observe herself? I think Nina's breakdown can be understood as a progression from being watched, to watching herself, to becoming unable to experience herself as anything other than an object of observation. Thomas watches her, her mother monitors her, the dancers compare themselves to one another. Early on, Nina uses mirrors to monitor and correct her body. As the film progresses, her reflections begin to move independently, distort, or become separate from her. Aronofsky repeatedly uses mirrors, fragmented close-ups, reflections, and voyeuristic camerawork to make us scrutinise Nina's body alongside her. So my question is: is Black Swan actually making us uncomfortable with the act of watching Nina, or does it ultimately turn her dissociation and suffering into something beautiful for us to consume?
label: analysis

text: I felt underwhelmed by Kurosawa's Ran. I don't hate Ran, and admire many things about it - the color palette in particular is incredible and makes some shots look like moving paintings. The battle for the third castle was intense and unlike anything I had seen on film before. Yet so much else about this film made me feel bored and detached. Many scenes are shot from a static camera that moves little if at all, and often positioned back away from the characters, making it feel at times more like a recording of a play than a movie. Taro and Jiro, the two oldest brothers, felt practically indistinguishable to me in terms of personality and motivation. Saburo is more interesting, and yet he is underutilized. Kaede is one of the most interesting characters in terms of her plotting and motivation, and yet in many scenes she is also stiff and flat. It felt like Kurosawa sacrificed the multidimensionality of characters in order to use them as props for cool shots.
label: analysis

text: On Obsession obsession. I saw Obsession opening weekend and like many was very impressed. I think it's a fantastic performance from Navarette and will undoubtedly make her a star, but I still had some issues with the male lead and some of the storytelling. Overall it was a very promising indie debut. All that said, I've been a little baffled by the response to it. A film of this scale outgrossing something like Sinners is admittedly a little surprising. I teach at a film school and have been asking my students about it, and none of my undergrad or graduate aged students seem to have more than a mild appreciation for it. I stumbled across the subreddit for the film this week and found people obsessively discussing fan theories and declaring it the greatest film in years. Does anyone else have any insights as to what exactly this movie has tapped into to get what I'm assuming are teens to the theater week over week for two months now? It's become an academic curiosity for me.

text: Just finished rewatching Burning (2018) - one of the movies where Director respects the audience. I must have watched this movie a while back and at that time I felt like it was clear that Ben was a serial killer for sure. But now that I have re-watched it, it left me with many layered questions about all the characters. First, our protagonist Jong Su - the whole movie is directed to make us feel like we are living and feeling everything that he is going through, like the shot change to POV when he sees the light in Hae-mi's room reflecting from the tower. Second, Hae-mi - we get two conflicting accounts from both Jong Su's mom and Hae-mi's parents about her falling in a well as a child, which makes me question whether she was actually killed or might just vanish "like a puff of smoke." Third, Ben - he is a person disconnected from all emotions who "plays" with others; maybe he knew Jong Su was following him and deliberately took him to the hill to play with his mind. Fourth, the director deliberately shoots many shots from Jong Su's POV, an intentional decision to make everyone feel biased towards his emotions.
label: analysis

text: Andy Warhol's Flesh (1968). I was surprised to find this movie had largely negative reviews both contemporarily and retrospectively. I loved it. It's mildly hammy, amateurish, lacking in plot. It's inhabited by various famous figures from the 'Warhol set' of 1960s New York, including Joe Dallesandro, Candy Darling, Jackie Curtis. The plot centers on Joe and his wife Geri needing to make $200 so they can pay for Geri's girlfriend's abortion, both of them sex workers. The director's explanation of the movie was that it's about all of the problems people have in relation to their flesh - the problem of having to sell your flesh to live, of having to bear flesh, of aging flesh, of being born with the 'wrong flesh'. The lines are blurred by the fact that many of the characters are essentially playing hammed up versions of themselves - Joe Dallesandro was a real-life sex worker and male model, for example, and drew from real-life experiences for his performance.
label: analysis

text: Unpopular: Ian is not that bad of a friend in Obsession. text: Reviewing Every Kurosawa Film: The Bad Sleep Well. News reporters swarm a wedding. Iwabuchi, the bride's father, is a high-ranking bureaucrat hounded by rumors of corruption. Toshiro Mifune is Nishi, Iwabuchi's new son-in-law and saboteur, whose desire for revenge is complicated by his genuine love for Iwabuchi's daughter. Wada becomes something of an audience surrogate, and through him we see Mifune's Nishi descend from a man intent on justice to one who glories in hurting those responsible for his father's death. Though the wedding is reminiscent of the wedding in The Godfather, The Bad Sleep Well feels functionally as much of a spy thriller as a crime story. This is one of the few Kurosawa films I hadn't seen previously, and the ending caught me off guard. Good men are shades of grey, and their imperfections make them vulnerable; truly evil men are bulletproof, because they have nothing that they care for enough to jeopardize their power. Grade: A-

text: Jennifer's Body, Megan Fox's Media Body and the Wish That Becomes a Curse in Obsession. I wrote a film-theory essay on Jennifer's Body and Curry Barker's Obsession, with Michel Tournier's Abel Tiffauges as a literary prelude. My reading of Jennifer's Body centers on Megan Fox's public image. Fox enters the film already carrying a media body made by 2000s Hollywood, a sex-symbol image built to withstand mass attention. Jennifer gives that image a fictional body, then gives it appetite. Low Shoulder treat Jennifer's body as a readable ritual object, as if beauty and supposed virginity could be converted into success. Their mistake is a fantasy of total interpretation. Obsession gives the same problem a more intimate form. Bear's wish begins as grief and the need to be confirmed by another person's love. Once the wish is granted, it stops behaving like a feeling. Nikki becomes the body occupied by Bear's externalized desire. The wish turns into a curse because it continues to appear after it has lost any human measure.
label: analysis
